claims.claim: DA proteins (i.e. CEP83, CEP89, FBF1, SCLT1, and CEP164) are essential for centriole-to-membrane docking and TTBK2 recruitment that promote ciliogenesis.
claims.source: DA proteins (i.e. CEP83, CEP89, FBF1, SCLT1, and CEP164) are essential for centriole-to-membrane docking and TTBK2 recruitment that promote ciliogenesis (Tanos et al., 2013; Huang et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Super-resolution microscopy has enabled researchers to identify the precise localization of centrosomal components, including those of the DA and SDA.
claims.source: Super-resolution microscopy has enabled researchers to identify the precise localization of centrosomal components, including those of the DA and SDA (Yang et al., 2018), and it has revealed that SDAs differ from DAs in both molecular composition and intracellular functions (Uzbekov and Alieva, 2018).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: SDAs differ from DAs in both molecular composition and intracellular functions.
claims.source: Super-resolution microscopy has enabled researchers to identify the precise localization of centrosomal components, including those of the DA and SDA (Yang et al., 2018), and it has revealed that SDAs differ from DAs in both molecular composition and intracellular functions (Uzbekov and Alieva, 2018).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: SDAs are composed of ODF2, CEP128, centriolin, NdelI, CCDC68, CCDC120, ninein, and CEP170, etc.
claims.source: Located beneath the DAs, SDAs are composed of ODF2, CEP128, centriolin, NdelI, CCDC68, CCDC120, ninein, and CEP170, etc. (Huang et al., 2017; Kashihara et al., 2019), and they are classified into two groups according to their specific localizations.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: SDA proteins are classified into two groups according to their specific localizations.
claims.source: Located beneath the DAs, SDAs are composed of ODF2, CEP128, centriolin, NdelI, CCDC68, CCDC120, ninein, and CEP170, etc. (Huang et al., 2017; Kashihara et al., 2019), and they are classified into two groups according to their specific localizations.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: The ODF group (ODF2, CEP128, and centriolin) is localized on SDAs only.
claims.source: The ODF group (ODF2, CEP128, and centriolin) is localized on SDAs only, whereas the ninein group (ninein, Kif2a, p150glued, CCDC68, CCDC120, and CEP170) are localized on both SDAs and the proximal ends of centrioles (Mazo et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: The ninein group (ninein, Kif2a, p150glued, CCDC68, CCDC120, and CEP170) are localized on both SDAs and the proximal ends of centrioles.
claims.source: The ODF group (ODF2, CEP128, and centriolin) is localized on SDAs only, whereas the ninein group (ninein, Kif2a, p150glued, CCDC68, CCDC120, and CEP170) are localized on both SDAs and the proximal ends of centrioles (Mazo et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: ODF2 occupies the bases of both the DAs and SDAs via different domains and thus participates in the hierarchical assembly of both DAs and SDAs.
claims.source: Of them, ODF2 occupies the bases of both the DAs and SDAs via different domains and thus participates in the hierarchical assembly of both DAs and SDAs (Tateishi et al., 2013; Chong et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: ODF2 ensures that microtubules focus properly at the centrosome, which then controls microtubule organization and stability.
claims.source: Also, ODF2 ensures that microtubules focus properly at the centrosome, which then controls microtubule organization and stability (Hung et al., 2016a), and centriolin, ninein, CCDC68, and CCDC120 are all required for microtubule stabilization and anchorage at the centrosomes (Gromley et al., 2003; Mogensen et al., 2000; Huang et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Centriolin, ninein, CCDC68, and CCDC120 are all required for microtubule stabilization and anchorage at the centrosomes.
claims.source: Also, ODF2 ensures that microtubules focus properly at the centrosome, which then controls microtubule organization and stability (Hung et al., 2016a), and centriolin, ninein, CCDC68, and CCDC120 are all required for microtubule stabilization and anchorage at the centrosomes (Gromley et al., 2003; Mogensen et al., 2000; Huang et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: The SDA proteins cooperate to form a microtubule anchoring complex that maintains the microtubule array.
claims.source: The SDA proteins cooperate to form a microtubule anchoring complex that maintains the microtubule array.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the known functions of individual SDA proteins cited in previous literature.

claims.claim: The taxilin family (i.e. α-taxilin, β-taxilin, and γ-taxilin) have been reported to interact with syntaxin family members and to participate in intracellular vesicle transport.
claims.source: The taxilin family (i.e. α-taxilin, β-taxilin, and γ-taxilin) have been reported to interact with syntaxin family members and to participate in intracellular vesicle transport (Nogami et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: α- and γ-taxilin form ring-like structures between CCDC120 and ninein.
claims.source: After they are recruited to SDA via ODF2, they form ring-like structures between CCDC120 and ninein, and participate in CEP170 assembly.
claims.evidence: This is supported by STED nanoscopy data showing the relative positions of these proteins.

claims.claim: α- and γ-taxilin participate in CEP170 assembly.
claims.source: After they are recruited to SDA via ODF2, they form ring-like structures between CCDC120 and ninein, and participate in CEP170 assembly.
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and functional studies showing interaction and recruitment of CEP170 by α-taxilin.

claims.claim: α- and γ-taxilin are involved in microtubule anchorage at the centrosome.
claims.source: Like other colleagues in the SDAs, α- and γ-taxilin are involved in microtubule anchorage at the centrosome and are also indispensable for spindle orientation during metaphase.
claims.evidence: This is supported by microtubule regrowth assays showing compromised microtubule reformation in taxilin-depleted cells.

claims.claim: α- and γ-taxilin are indispensable for spindle orientation during metaphase.
claims.source: Like other colleagues in the SDAs, α- and γ-taxilin are involved in microtubule anchorage at the centrosome and are also indispensable for spindle orientation during metaphase.
claims.evidence: This is supported by spindle orientation measurements showing increased spindle angles in taxilin knockout cells.

claims.claim: APEX2-mediated proximal labeling uses hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) as an oxidant to catalyze biotin-phenol (BP), a small molecular substrate, to produce the reactive BP radical that conjugates to the endogenous proteins that are proximal to APEX2.
claims.source: APEX2-mediated proximal labeling is an approach that uses hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) as an oxidant to catalyze biotin-phenol (BP), a small molecular substrate, to produce the reactive BP radical that conjugates to the endogenous proteins that are proximal to APEX2 (Hung et al., 2016b).
claims.evidence: This is a methodological description supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: CCDC68 and CCDC120 were previously identified as SDA components.
claims.source: To search for new SDA components, we labeled two previously identified SDA components CCDC68 and CCDC120 (Huang et al., 2017) by infusing them with V5-tagged APEX2.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Overexpressed V5-tagged CCDC68 and CCDC120 fusion proteins showed a ring (top view) or three dots (side view) at the centrosome.
claims.source: When overexpressed in HeLa cells, the V5 immunostained CCDC68 and CCDC120 fusion proteins showed a ring (top view) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) or three dots (side view) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) at the centrosome, results that were consistent with their SDA locations when they had been stained by their specific antibodies (Huang et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B.

claims.claim: APEX2-mediated biotinylation successfully marked the endogenous proteins around CCDC68 or CCDC120 at the centrosomes.
claims.source: After treatment with BP and H2O2, the biotinylated endogenous proteins co-localized and encircled V5-tagged CCDC120 or V5-tagged CCDC68 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B), thus indicating that APEX2-mediated biotinylation had successfully marked the endogenous proteins around CCDC68 or CCDC120 at the centrosomes.
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B.

claims.claim: Samples without BP or H2O2 showed no biotinylation signal.
claims.source: As a negative control, samples without BP or H2O2 showed no biotinylation signal.
claims.evidence: This is a control experiment result that validates the specificity of the APEX2-mediated biotinylation approach.

claims.claim: Immunoblotting results confirmed the endogenous biotinylated proteins mediated by CCDC68 and CCDC120 proximal labeling.
claims.source: Furthermore, immunoblotting results also confirmed the endogenous biotinylated proteins mediated by CCDC68 and CCDC120 proximal labeling (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-D.

claims.claim: A series of previously identified centriolar proteins were found among the candidates for CCDC68 and CCDC120 proximal labeling, verifying the efficiency of the centrosomal proteomics approach.
claims.source: Among those candidates for CCDC68 and CCDC120 proximal labeling, a series of previously identified centriolar proteins (marked in green in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) were found, and thus verified the efficiency of our centrosomal proteomics approach.
claims.evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: Several centrosomal proteins possess the coiled-coil domain that is the basis for the protein-protein interactions essential for centrosome configuration.
claims.source: Since several centrosomal proteins possess the coiled-coil domain that is the basis for the protein-protein interactions essential for centrosome configuration (Andersen et al., 2003), we focused on proteins containing one or more coiled-coil domains.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Five new proteins, including α-taxilin, DACT1, DRG2, NCAPH2, and SMAP2, were found co-localized with centrosome markers CP110 or γ-tubulin.
claims.source: Other than the already known centrosome proteins, five new proteins, including α-taxilin, DACT1, DRG2, NCAPH2, and SMAP2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F), were found co-localized with centrosome markers CP110 or γ-tubulin, thus proving that they resided on centrosomes.
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: DRG2 was found in both CCDC68 and CCDC120 proximal candidates.
claims.source: Among them, DRG2 was found in both CCDC68 and CCDC120 proximal candidates; α-taxilin, NCAPH2, and SMAP2 were found in CCDC68 proximal candidates; and DACT1 was found in CCDC120 proximal candidates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E-F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E-F.

claims.claim: α-taxilin, NCAPH2, and SMAP2 were found in CCDC68 proximal candidates.
claims.source: Among them, DRG2 was found in both CCDC68 and CCDC120 proximal candidates; α-taxilin, NCAPH2, and SMAP2 were found in CCDC68 proximal candidates; and DACT1 was found in CCDC120 proximal candidates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E-F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E-F.

claims.claim: DACT1 was found in CCDC120 proximal candidates.
claims.source: Among them, DRG2 was found in both CCDC68 and CCDC120 proximal candidates; α-taxilin, NCAPH2, and SMAP2 were found in CCDC68 proximal candidates; and DACT1 was found in CCDC120 proximal candidates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E-F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E-F.

claims.claim: γ-taxilin co-localized with Nek2A at the centrosome during interphase.
claims.source: A previous study had shown γ-taxilin co-localized with Nek2A at the centrosome during interphase (Makiyama et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: γ-taxilin co-localized with γ-tubulin.
claims.source: The immunofluorescence assay showed it co-localized with γ-tubulin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), thus confirming its centrosomal localization.
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: α-taxilin and γ-taxilin are similar in that their middle regions each has a long coiled-coil domain.
claims.source: Among the proteins that showed centrosomal localization, α- and γ-taxilin are similar in that their middle regions each has a long coiled-coil domain (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A; Makiyama et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by protein domain analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: The anti-α-taxilin antibody was designed to recognize the C-terminus of α-taxilin.
claims.source: Both the anti-α-taxilin antibody and anti-γ-taxilin antibody, which were designed to recognize the C-terminus of each of those proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-C), were chosen to detect their specificities.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological description supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-C.

claims.claim: The anti-γ-taxilin antibody was designed to recognize the C-terminus of γ-taxilin.
claims.source: Both the anti-α-taxilin antibody and anti-γ-taxilin antibody, which were designed to recognize the C-terminus of each of those proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-C), were chosen to detect their specificities.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological description supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-C.

claims.claim: α-taxilin's molecular weight is above 72 kDa, which is slightly higher than predicted.
claims.source: Immunoblotting results showed that the two proteins' molecular weights (above 72 kDa for α-taxilin and about 70 kDa for γ-taxilin) were slightly higher than predicted (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B-C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B-C.

claims.claim: γ-taxilin's molecular weight is about 70 kDa, which is slightly higher than predicted.
claims.source: Immunoblotting results showed that the two proteins' molecular weights (above 72 kDa for α-taxilin and about 70 kDa for γ-taxilin) were slightly higher than predicted (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B-C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B-C.

claims.claim: Immunoblotting detected significant decreases in the amount of α-taxilin and γ-taxilin after siRNA knockdown.
claims.source: Immunoblotting also detected significant decreases in the amount of those proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B-C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B-C.

claims.claim: α-taxilin and γ-taxilin stained by their antibodies focused prominently at the centrosome, as indicated by their co-localizations with γ-tubulin in human RPE-1 cells.
claims.source: The immunofluorescence assay showed that α-taxilin and γ-taxilin stained by their antibodies focused prominently at the centrosome, as indicated by their co-localizations with γ-tubulin in human RPE-1 cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data.

claims.claim: The fluorescence intensities of both α-taxilin and γ-taxilin decreased at the centrosome after siRNA knockdown.
claims.source: Also, the fluorescence intensities of both taxilins decreased at the centrosome after siRNA knockdown (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claims.claim: In the G1 phase, the top views of α- and γ-taxilin showed their ring-like patterns encompassing one centrin-3 dot that resides in the distal lumen of centrioles.
claims.source: In the G1 phase, the top views of α- and γ-taxilin showed their ring-like patterns encompassing one centrin-3 dot that resides in the distal lumen of centrioles (Middendorp et al., 1997; Figure 1A–B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by 3D-SIM imaging data shown in Figure 1A-B and citation to previous literature about centrin-3 localization.

claims.claim: The α- and γ-taxilin side views showed three dots occupying two levels with one level (two dots) beside ODF2 and thus at the SDA.
claims.source: The α- and γ-taxilin side views showed three dots occupying two levels with one level (two dots) beside ODF2 and thus at the SDA (Figure 1A–B), and the other level (one dot) assumed to be at the proximal end (Figure 1A–E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by 3D-SIM imaging data shown in Figure 1A-E.

claims.claim: The other level of α- and γ-taxilin (one dot) is assumed to be at the proximal end.
claims.source: The α- and γ-taxilin side views showed three dots occupying two levels with one level (two dots) beside ODF2 and thus at the SDA (Figure 1A–B), and the other level (one dot) assumed to be at the proximal end (Figure 1A–E).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the localization pattern observed in 3D-SIM imaging data shown in Figure 1A-E.

claims.claim: α- and γ-taxilin patterns resembled those of the ninein group, such as ninein and CEP170.
claims.source: Those patterns resembled those of the ninein group, such as ninein and CEP170 (Mazo et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison to previously characterized localization patterns supported by citation.

claims.claim: α-taxilin clearly co-localized with the ninein and CEP170 rings in the top view, and with the three ninein and/or CEP170 dots in the side view.
claims.source: Indeed, α-taxilin clearly co-localized with the ninein and CEP170 rings in the top view, and with the three ninein and/or CEP170 dots in the side view (Figure 1C and E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by 3D-SIM imaging data shown in Figure 1C and E.

claims.claim: γ-taxilin patterns resembled those of α-taxilin by containing a smaller ring that resided inside the ninein and CEP170 signals.
claims.source: Corresponding γ-taxilin patterns resembled those of α-taxilin by containing a smaller ring that resided inside the ninein and CEP170 signals (Figure 1D and F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by 3D-SIM imaging data shown in Figure 1D and F.

claims.claim: α-taxilin's M2 deletion (261–300 aa) eliminated its localization at the SDA.
claims.source: The immunofluorescence assay showed that the M2 deletion (261–300 aa) in α-taxilin eliminated its localization at the SDA, and deletion of M3 (301–350 aa) and M4 (351–400 aa) eliminated its localization at the proximal end (Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: Deletion of α-taxilin's M3 (301–350 aa) and M4 (351–400 aa) eliminated its localization at the proximal end.
claims.source: The immunofluorescence assay showed that the M2 deletion (261–300 aa) in α-taxilin eliminated its localization at the SDA, and deletion of M3 (301–350 aa) and M4 (351–400 aa) eliminated its localization at the proximal end (Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: Other deletion mutants of α-taxilin (i.e. the N-terminus [1–185 aa], the C-terminus [492–546 aa] and M1 [186–260 aa]) did not affect α-taxilin's centrosomal localization patterns.
claims.source: Other deletion mutants (i.e. the N-terminus [1–185 aa], the C-terminus [492–546 aa] and M1 [186–260 aa]) did not affect α-taxilin's centrosomal localization patterns (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: α-taxilin's M2 is responsible for its SDA localization.
claims.source: These data suggest that α-taxilin's M2 is responsible for its SDA localization, while M3 and M4 are required for its proximal end localization.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the deletion mutant analysis data.

claims.claim: α-taxilin's M3 and M4 are required for its proximal end localization.
claims.source: These data suggest that α-taxilin's M2 is responsible for its SDA localization, while M3 and M4 are required for its proximal end localization.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the deletion mutant analysis data.

claims.claim: For γ-taxilin, M1 (228–270 aa) is responsible for its localization at the proximal end.
claims.source: For γ-taxilin, M1 (228–270 aa) is responsible for its localization at the proximal end, while M2 (271–317 aa) is responsible for its SDA localization (Figure 1J and Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1J and Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claims.claim: For γ-taxilin, M2 (271–317 aa) is responsible for its SDA localization.
claims.source: For γ-taxilin, M1 (228–270 aa) is responsible for its localization at the proximal end, while M2 (271–317 aa) is responsible for its SDA localization (Figure 1J and Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1J and Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claims.claim: The ODF2 ring had the smallest diameter among the SDA proteins examined.
claims.source: Of those, the ODF2 ring had the smallest diameter and the rest of those proteins' rings increased in size in this order: CCDC68, CCDC120, γ-taxilin, α-taxilin, ninein, and CEP170 (Figure 2A–B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by STED nanoscopy imaging and diameter measurements shown in Figure 2A-B.

claims.claim: SDA protein rings increased in size in this order: ODF2, CCDC68, CCDC120, γ-taxilin, α-taxilin, ninein, and CEP170.
claims.source: Of those, the ODF2 ring had the smallest diameter and the rest of those proteins' rings increased in size in this order: CCDC68, CCDC120, γ-taxilin, α-taxilin, ninein, and CEP170 (Figure 2A–B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by STED nanoscopy imaging and diameter measurements shown in Figure 2A-B.

claims.claim: SDA proteins formed ordered concentric circles beginning with ODF2 and ending with CEP170 in the following order: ODF2, CCDC68, CCDC120, γ-taxilin, α-taxilin, ninein, and CEP170.
claims.source: Therefore, those SDA proteins formed ordered concentric circles beginning with ODF2 and ending with CEP170 in the following order: ODF2, CCDC68, CCDC120, γ-taxilin, α-taxilin, ninein, and CEP170.

claims.claim: The top view of the SDA region showed that α- and γ-taxilin encircled the ODF2 ring.

claims.claim: When viewed from the side, α- and γ-taxilin localized proximal to ODF2's upper level.

claims.evidence: This is supported by STED nanoscopy imaging shown in Figure 3C-D.

claims.claim: When ODF2 was depleted by siRNA knockdown, α- and γ-taxilin levels in those cells did not change significantly.

claims.claim: Fluorescence intensity of both α- and γ-taxilin decreased at the centrosomes after ODF2 depletion.

claims.claim: ODF2 affects α- and γ-taxilin centrosomal localizations without affecting their protein levels.

claims.claim: Lost SDA signals of α-taxilin and γ-taxilin could be rescued by overexpressing full-length ODF2.

claims.claim: The ODF2 1–59 aa deletion mutant affects ODF2 localization at the SDA.
claims.source: However, the 1–59 aa deletion mutant, which affects ODF2 localization at the SDA (Tateishi et al., 2013) and recruitment of other SDA components (Huang et al., 2017), could not rescue SDA localization of either α-taxilin or γ-taxilin after siRNA treatment (Figure 3H–I).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: The ODF2 1–59 aa deletion mutant affects recruitment of other SDA components.

claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: The ODF2 1–59 aa deletion mutant could not rescue SDA localization of either α-taxilin or γ-taxilin after siRNA treatment.

claims.evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 3H-I.

claims.claim: Ectopically expressed CCDC68 and CCDC120 could not be immunoprecipitated from cell lysates by ectopically expressed α-taxilin or γ-taxilin in HEK-293T cells.
claims.source: In contrast, depleted CCDC68 or CCDC120 did not affect α-taxilin or γ-taxilin fluorescence intensity at centrosomes in RPE-1 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-F), and ectopically expressed CCDC68 and CCDC120 could not be immunoprecipitated from cell lysates by ectopically expressed α-taxilin or γ-taxilin in HEK-293T cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G-J).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G-J.

claims.claim: TCHP was reported to reside at the SDA midzone and to interact with ODF2 and ninein.
claims.source: Previously, TCHP was reported to reside at the SDA midzone and to interact with ODF2 and ninein (Ibi et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Endogenous TCHP did not interact with either α-taxilin or γ-taxilin in HEK-293T cells.
claims.source: Here, endogenous TCHP did not interact with either α-taxilin or γ-taxilin in HEK-293T cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1K).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1K.

claims.claim: The proper localization of α-taxilin and γ-taxilin at the SDA depends on ODF2, but not on CCDC68, CCDC120, or TCHP.
claims.source: Therefore, the proper localization of α-taxilin and γ-taxilin at the SDA depends on ODF2, but not on CCDC68, CCDC120, or TCHP.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the combined data from depletion and immunoprecipitation experiments.

claims.claim: α-taxilin and γ-taxilin belong to the taxilin family and each possesses a coiled-coil domain in their middle regions.
claims.source: We then moved on to determine the relationship between α-taxilin and γ-taxilin, which belong to the taxilin family and each possesses a coiled-coil domain in their middle regions (Nogami et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: An interaction between α-taxilin and γ-taxilin was detected after immunoprecipitation in HEK-293T cells.
claims.source: First, we detected an interaction between those two proteins after immunoprecipitation in HEK-293T cells (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: α-taxilin fluorescence intensity was less at the γ-taxilin KO cell centrosomes compared with that of wild-type (WT) cells.

claims.claim: α-taxilin depletion did not affect centrosomal γ-taxilin fluorescence intensity.

claims.claim: γ-taxilin directly recruits α-taxilin to centrosomes via its coiled-coil domain.

claims.claim: Ninein and CEP170 occupy the peripheral region of the SDA structure.
claims.source: The SDA marker proteins ninein and CEP170 occupy the peripheral region of the SDA structure (Huang et al., 2017; Chong et al., 2020), and based on the SDA protein localization pattern, α-taxilin is located upstream of those two proteins (Figure 2A).

claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the localization data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: α-taxilin interacted with CEP170 but not with ninein.
claims.source: An endogenous immunoprecipitation assay showed that α-taxilin interacted with CEP170 but not with ninein (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: CEP170 interacted with α-taxilin in cells overexpressing full-length α-taxilin, as well as the M (186–491 aa) region and C-terminus (491–546 aa) deletion mutant constructs (ΔC), but not with the N-terminus construct (1–185 aa).

claims.claim: The α-taxilin M region, but not the N- or C-terminal regions, is required for its interaction with CEP170.

claims.claim: α-taxilin may directly bind CEP170.

claims.claim: A significant decrease in CEP170 fluorescence intensity was detected in RPE-1 cells treated with α-taxilin siRNA, compared with control siRNA.

claims.claim: The α-taxilin deletion mutant (ΔM2) lacking the region responsible for its SDA localization failed to rescue the CEP170 fluorescence intensity at the centrosomes.

claims.evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 5E-F.

claims.claim: α-taxilin participates with CEP170 in SDA assembly.
claims.source: These results indicate that α-taxilin participates with CEP170 in SDA assembly.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the combined data from interaction studies and functional assays.

claims.claim: In WT RPE-1 cells, the side view showed that SDA stems were beside centriole wall and that they occupied a wide range at the subdistal position of the mother centriole.

claims.claim: The smallest SDAs appeared in γ-taxilin KO RPE-1 cells.

claims.source: These results suggest an indispensable role of α-taxilin and γ-taxilin in maintaining SDA integrity.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the TEM data showing reduced SDA size in knockout cells.

claims.claim: The microtubule asters were significantly impaired in the α-taxilin and γ-taxilin KO RPE-1 cells.

claims.claim: The microtubule array densities were obviously less in α-taxilin and γ-taxilin KO RPE-1 cells.

claims.evidence: This is supported by microtubule regrowth assay data shown in Figure 6B and D.

claims.claim: Compromised microtubule reformation was observed in α-taxilin and γ-taxilin siRNA-depleted RPE-1 cells, compared with control cells.

Those results displayed compromised microtubule reformation in the experimental cells, compared with that in the control cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by microtubule regrowth assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-E.

claims.claim: The compromised microtubule regrowth, triggered by depletion of α-taxilin or γ-taxilin, could be partly rescued by overexpression of 3×FLAG-tagged full-length α-taxilin or γ-taxilin.
claims.source: The compromised microtubule regrowth, triggered by depletion of α-taxilin or γ-taxilin, could be partly rescued by overexpression of 3×FLAG-tagged full-length α-taxilin or γ-taxilin, but not by the M2 region (Figure 1G–H) deletion mutants of either taxilin (Figure 6B–E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 6B-E.

claims.claim: The compromised microtubule regrowth could not be rescued by the M2 region deletion mutants of either α-taxilin or γ-taxilin.

claims.evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 6B-E.

claims.claim: The SDA localization of both α-taxilin and γ-taxilin have indispensible roles in controlling microtubule anchoring at the interphase centrosome.

claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiment data showing that M2 deletion mutants cannot rescue the microtubule regrowth defect.

claims.claim: γ-Tubulin, as a member of the γ-TuRC complex, plays a major role in microtubule nucleation.
claims.source: The centrosome acts as an MTOC by controlling microtubule nucleation and anchoring. γ-Tubulin, as a member of the γ-TuRC complex, plays a major role in microtubule nucleation (Schatten and Sun, 2018).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: The γ-tubulin fluorescence intensity at the interphase centrosome remained unchanged following both α-taxilin and γ-taxilin siRNA-induced depletion.

claims.evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F-G.

claims.claim: Microtubule nucleation may not be affected by α-taxilin and γ-taxilin depletion.
claims.source: The γ-tubulin fluorescence intensity at the interphase centrosome remained unchanged following both α-taxilin and γ-taxilin siRNA-induced depletion (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F-G), thus suggesting that microtubule nucleation may not be affected.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the γ-tubulin fluorescence intensity data, though stated as speculative ('may not').

claims.claim: Bipolar spindle formation was not affected in both α- and γ-taxilin KO cells.

claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Changes in the orientation of the spindle to the substratum were obvious in α- and γ-taxilin KO cells.
claims.source: Although bipolar spindle formation was not affected in both α- and γ-taxilin KO cells (Figure 7C), changes in the orientation of the spindle to the substratum were obvious (Figure 7C–E).

claims.claim: The average spindle angle increased from 4.94 (0.46)° in WT cells to 10.94 (0.93)° in γ-taxilin KO cells.

claims.evidence: This is supported by spindle angle measurement data shown in Figure 7D-E.

claims.claim: Spindle misorientations were not rescued by the M2 deletion mutant for each taxilin.

claims.evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 7C-E.

claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.evidence: This is supported by aster microtubule length measurement data shown in Figure 7F-G.

claims.claim: Aster microtubule lengths in the α-taxilin (2.20 [0.07] μm) and γ-taxilin (2.19 [0.07] μm) KO HeLa cells were significantly less than in WT cells.
claims.source: While the WT's aster microtubule length was 3.09 (SE 0.07) μm, those lengths in the α-taxilin (2.20 [0.07] μm) and γ-taxilin (2.19 [0.07] μm) KO HeLa cells were significantly less (Figure 7F–G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by aster microtubule length measurement data shown in Figure 7F-G.

claims.claim: The changes in spindle orientation observed in α-taxilin and γ-taxilin KO HeLa cells are likely caused by decreased astral microtubule length.

results.result: α-taxilin and γ-taxilin are newly identified SDA components that localize to the subdistal appendage of the mother centriole. Using APEX2-mediated proximity labeling with CCDC68 and CCDC120 as baits, followed by mass spectrometry, the authors identified α-taxilin among new centrosomal proteins. Super-resolution microscopy (3D-SIM) revealed that both α- and γ-taxilin form ring-like structures at the SDA and show three-dot patterns in side views, with localization patterns resembling the ninein group.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C37-C38, C40-C41, C43, C48, C55, C57-C58, C61-C62 provide converging evidence from multiple experimental approaches. The APEX2 proximity labeling successfully identified α-taxilin (C37-C38, C40-C41), which was validated by immunofluorescence showing centrosomal localization (C43, C48, C55). Super-resolution microscopy data (C57-C58, C61-C62) demonstrate the specific SDA localization pattern. The combination of proteomics, immunofluorescence, and super-resolution imaging provides strong support for this result.

results.result: α-taxilin and γ-taxilin form a complex via their coiled-coil domains, with γ-taxilin recruiting α-taxilin to the centrosome. Immunoprecipitation experiments detected interaction between the two proteins (C104), and knockout of γ-taxilin reduced α-taxilin centrosomal localization (C105) but not vice versa (C106). Domain mapping showed the interaction occurs through coiled-coil domains (C107), confirmed by in vitro binding assays (C108).
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C103-C109 provide strong evidence through multiple complementary approaches. The immunoprecipitation data (C104), knockout cell analysis showing asymmetric dependency (C105-C106), domain mapping (C107), and in vitro binding assays (C108) all converge to support the conclusion that γ-taxilin directly recruits α-taxilin via coiled-coil domain interactions. The asymmetric dependency (γ-taxilin KO affects α-taxilin but not vice versa) is particularly compelling evidence for the hierarchical relationship.

results.result: The SDA localization of α-taxilin and γ-taxilin depends on ODF2. Immunoprecipitation showed ODF2 interacts with both taxilins (C87), and STED imaging revealed taxilins encircle the ODF2 ring (C88-C89). ODF2 depletion by siRNA reduced taxilin centrosomal localization without affecting protein levels (C90-C92), specifically eliminating SDA signals while preserving proximal end signals (C93). Full-length ODF2 rescued the phenotype, but an ODF2 deletion mutant (Δ1-59aa) did not (C94, C97).
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C87-C94, C97, C102 provide strong evidence through interaction studies, localization analysis, depletion experiments, and rescue experiments. The combination of immunoprecipitation (C87), super-resolution imaging (C88-C89), siRNA knockdown showing specific loss of SDA localization (C90-C93), and domain-specific rescue experiments (C94, C97) provides compelling support. The specificity of the ODF2 N-terminus requirement strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: α-taxilin recruits CEP170 to the SDA through direct interaction. Immunoprecipitation showed α-taxilin interacts with CEP170 but not ninein (C112), and STED imaging confirmed co-localization at SDAs and proximal ends (C113). Domain mapping identified the α-taxilin M region as necessary for CEP170 interaction (C114-C115), supported by in vitro binding assays (C116). α-taxilin depletion reduced CEP170 centrosomal localization (C117), which was rescued by full-length α-taxilin but not by the ΔM2 mutant lacking SDA localization (C118-C119).
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C112-C120 provide strong evidence through interaction studies, localization analysis, domain mapping, and functional rescue experiments. The immunoprecipitation data (C112), STED co-localization (C113), domain mapping (C114-C115), in vitro binding (C116), and rescue experiments with domain-specific mutants (C117-C119) all converge to support the conclusion. The specificity of the rescue (full-length works, ΔM2 doesn't) is particularly compelling.

results.result: α-taxilin and γ-taxilin occupy a distinct middle zone within the SDA structure, positioned between CCDC120 and ninein. STED nanoscopy revealed that SDA proteins form ordered concentric circles with increasing diameters: ODF2, CCDC68, CCDC120, γ-taxilin, α-taxilin, ninein, and CEP170 (C70-C72). Longitudinal position measurements showed γ-taxilin is higher and α-taxilin is lower than other SDA proteins (C84-C85), placing them in concentric circles between CCDC120 and ninein (C82-C83).
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C85, C154 are supported by quantitative STED nanoscopy measurements of both radial (diameter) and longitudinal positions. The systematic measurement of multiple SDA proteins (C70-C72) provides a comprehensive spatial map, and the specific positioning of taxilins between CCDC120 and ninein (C82-C83) with distinct longitudinal positions (C84-C85) is well-documented. The data establish a clear hierarchical organization of the SDA structure.

results.result: α-taxilin and γ-taxilin are essential for maintaining SDA structural integrity. Transmission electron microscopy of knockout cells revealed that α-taxilin KO cells showed narrower SDAs with smaller sizes (C122), while γ-taxilin KO cells showed the smallest SDAs (C123), compared to wild-type cells where SDAs occupied a wide range at the subdistal position (C121).
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C121-C124 are supported by TEM imaging data showing progressive reduction in SDA size from WT to α-taxilin KO to γ-taxilin KO cells. The quantitative measurements of SDA area (referenced in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) provide objective evidence. However, the claim would be strengthened by reporting the statistical significance and effect sizes of the SDA size reductions.

results.result: α-taxilin and γ-taxilin are required for centrosomal microtubule anchorage during interphase. Microtubule regrowth assays showed significantly impaired microtubule asters and reduced array densities in α-taxilin and γ-taxilin KO cells (C125-C126), confirmed in siRNA-depleted cells (C127). The defect was rescued by full-length taxilins but not by M2 deletion mutants lacking SDA localization (C128-C129). γ-tubulin intensity remained unchanged after taxilin depletion (C132), suggesting microtubule nucleation is not affected (C133).
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C125-C130, C132-C133 are supported by microtubule regrowth assays in both KO and siRNA-depleted cells, with quantitative measurements at multiple time points (0, 5, 10 min). The rescue experiments with domain-specific mutants (C128-C129) demonstrate that SDA localization is necessary for function. The unchanged γ-tubulin intensity (C132) provides evidence that the defect is in anchoring rather than nucleation, though this inference (C133) is stated cautiously as 'may not be affected.'

results.result: α-taxilin and γ-taxilin are required for proper spindle orientation during metaphase. While bipolar spindle formation was unaffected (C134), spindle orientation was significantly altered in KO cells (C135), with average spindle angles increasing from ~5° in WT to ~12° in α-taxilin KO and ~11° in γ-taxilin KO cells (C136-C137). The defect was rescued by full-length taxilins and proximal end deletion mutants (M3/M1) but not by SDA localization deletion mutants (M2) (C138-C140). Astral microtubule length was significantly reduced in KO cells (C143-C144), likely causing the spindle misorientation (C145).
results.evaluation: Claims C12, C134-C145 are supported by quantitative spindle angle measurements in KO cells with statistical analysis (C136-C137), rescue experiments with domain-specific mutants (C138-C140), and astral microtubule length measurements (C143-C144). The specificity of the rescue (M3/M1 mutants work, M2 mutants don't) demonstrates that SDA localization is critical for spindle orientation. The correlation with reduced astral microtubule length (C144-C145) provides a mechanistic link, though the causal inference (C145) is appropriately stated as 'likely.'

results.result: Specific domains of α-taxilin and γ-taxilin are responsible for their SDA and proximal end localizations. For α-taxilin, the M2 region (261-300 aa) is responsible for SDA localization (C63, C66), while M3 (301-350 aa) and M4 (351-400 aa) are required for proximal end localization (C64, C67). For γ-taxilin, M1 (228-270 aa) is responsible for proximal end localization (C68), while M2 (271-317 aa) is responsible for SDA localization (C69). Other deletion mutants did not affect localization patterns (C65).
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C69 are supported by systematic deletion mutant analysis with immunofluorescence imaging. The specificity of the domain requirements is demonstrated by testing multiple deletion constructs (C65) and showing that only specific regions affect localization. The data provide clear structure-function relationships for both proteins.

results.result: The SDA localization of α-taxilin and γ-taxilin is independent of CCDC68, CCDC120, and TCHP. Depletion of CCDC68 or CCDC120 did not affect taxilin centrosomal localization (C98), and no interaction was detected between taxilins and CCDC68/CCDC120 by immunoprecipitation (C99). Similarly, TCHP did not interact with either taxilin (C101).
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C99, C101-C102 are supported by negative results from both depletion experiments and immunoprecipitation assays. While negative results require careful interpretation, the combination of approaches (depletion and interaction studies) and the contrast with the positive ODF2 results (C87-C97) provide confidence in the conclusion that taxilin localization is independent of these proteins.

results.result: α-taxilin and γ-taxilin knockout results in centrosome disjunction. γ-taxilin KO caused centrosome disjunction in RPE-1 and HeLa cells (C179), and α-taxilin depletion produced a similar phenotype (C180). This suggests the proximal presence of taxilins may function as centrosome linkers regulating centrosome cohesion (C181).
results.evaluation: Claims C179-C180 are supported by imaging data showing increased percentages of cells with separated centrosomes (>2 μm) in both α-taxilin and γ-taxilin KO cells. The data are consistent with previous literature on γ-taxilin (C178). However, the mechanistic interpretation (C181) is appropriately stated as speculative ('may work as'), as the study did not directly test the centrosome linker hypothesis.

results.result: APEX2-mediated proximity labeling successfully identified centrosomal proteins near CCDC68 and CCDC120. The method uses H2O2 to catalyze biotin-phenol to produce reactive radicals that conjugate to proximal proteins (C35). Using previously identified SDA components CCDC68 and CCDC120 as baits (C36), the approach successfully labeled endogenous proteins, as validated by negative controls without BP or H2O2 (C39) and identification of known centrosomal proteins (C150).
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C36, C39, C150 describe the methodological approach and its validation. The method is well-established (C35 cites previous literature), and the validation through negative controls (C39) and identification of known proteins (C150) demonstrates technical success. This provides confidence in the novel proteins identified, including α-taxilin.

results.result: Some known SDA proteins were not detected in the APEX2 proximity labeling, likely due to technical limitations. ODF2, ninein, and CEP170 were not in the datasets, probably because of low protein levels (ODF2) or longer distances from the baits (ninein and CEP170) (C151). The interaction between ODF2 and CCDC120 may not be direct (C158), and interactions between ODF2 and taxilins are likely indirect given the size differences (C161).
results.evaluation: Claims C151, C158, C161 are speculative explanations for negative or indirect results. While the explanations are plausible (proximity labeling has distance limitations, protein abundance affects detection), they are not directly tested. The speculation about indirect interactions (C158, C161) is reasonable given the structural data but lacks direct experimental support such as yeast two-hybrid or in vitro binding assays between ODF2 and taxilins.
